content:
**Subject and central claims.** This section of Steven Pinker's *How the Mind Works* argues that thoughts are compositional: they are assembled from concepts bound to roles, not stored whole. File page 74 gives the reasoning. A node per whole thought yields a combinatorial explosion (the chessboard wheat legend: four trillion bushels), and the systematic pattern of thinkable thoughts — baby eats slug, slug eats baby, baby sees slug — resembles a matrix whose rows and columns indicate smaller components, as the periodic table indicated atomic structure. Pinker's conclusion: "Thoughts are assembled out of concepts; they are not stored whole" (file page 74).

**Why simple association fails.** Assigning units to concept-role pairs loses who-did-what-to-whom ("The baby ate the chicken when the poodle ate the slug" becomes indistinguishable from its swap; file page 74). Separate role pools with an auto-associator can complete "baby ate slug" from two components, but the four sentences "baby same-as baby," "baby different-from slug," "slug different-from baby," "slug same-as slug" pose an exclusive-or problem no weight setting solves (file pages 74–75). Pinker infers the mind needs a representation for the proposition itself; Geoffrey Hinton's model adds a proposition-unit layer whose arbitrary patterns act like serial numbers holding concepts in slots (file page 75). His explicit limit: logic's ingredients — predicate, argument, proposition — must be "snuck back in"; "association-stuff by itself is not enough" (file page 75).

**Quantification and binding.** Variable-binding distinguishes "a particular baby ate a particular slug" from generic readings; jokes and Lincoln's "you can't fool all the people all the time" depend on it (file page 75). Logicians use variables and quantifiers with precise ordering and bracketing, as in "Every forty-five seconds {there exists an X [who gets injured]}" versus "There exists an X {who every forty-five seconds [gets injured]}" (file page 76). Pinker states plainly: "so far, we have no hint as to how this can be done in an associative network" (file page 76).

**Interference and memory.** Superposition breeds cross-talk: Neal Cohen and Michael McCloskey's network, trained to add 2 after adding 1, became "amnesic for how to add 1" — catastrophic forgetting (file page 76). McClelland and Alan Kawamoto's ambiguous-sentence network produced the chimera humans never do: a winged mammal broke the window with a baseball bat (file page 76). Pinker notes generalization from dense interconnection is also the source of blending, and suggests each proposition may need its own storage slot and address (file page 76). David Sherry and Dan Schacter argue conflicting memory demands drove specialized systems: Clark's Nutcrackers cache in ten thousand places, nightingales learn two hundred songs, in different brain structures (file page 76). Humans need both episodic memory (episodes stamped with time, date, serial number) and semantic memory for generic knowledge, following Endel Tulving's distinction (file page 76).

**Recursion.** Embedding propositions in propositions yields a hierarchical tree and infinitely many thoughts, as adding one generates infinitely many numbers (file pages 76–77). Hard-wiring a network per nesting depth is clumsy; Pinker favors a recursive transition network, where each structure is stored once and a processor threads through it, storing its itinerary in short-term memory (file page 77). Michael Jordan and Jeff Elman's looping networks show iteration but "not enough to interpret or assemble structured propositions"; only specially assembled networks handle recursion (file page 77).

**Fuzzy versus crisp categories.** Ludwig Wittgenstein's "game" and Opus the Penguin show categories without necessary and sufficient features, organized around prototypes; people recognize stereotypes faster and even "see" them (file pages 77–78). An auto-associator computing property correlations matches this, suggesting "parts of human memory are wired something like an auto-associator" (file page 78). Yet people are also crisp: Sharon Armstrong, Henry Gleitman, and Lila Gleitman's students rated 13 a better odd number than 23, then denied gray areas (file page 78). Pinker posits two modes: soaking up correlations, and building intuitive theories — rule systems (kinship, law, arithmetic, grammar) that treat members equally and license explanation-based conclusions (file page 78). The section ends mid-critique of Hinton, Rumelhart, and McClelland's claim that similarity-based generalization is automatic, noting it "breaks down in any domain in which a person actually" reasons (file page 78).

**Engineering implications (mine, not Pinker's).** A thinking machine needs explicit role-binding structures, a proposition-level store with addresses to prevent catastrophic forgetting, a variable-binding mechanism (unimplemented in the source), a recursive transition processor over shared structures, and dual memory: timestamped episodic records plus semantic rules. Prototype similarity can seed generalization, but rule systems must override it. The source supplies the failure analyses and representational requirements; it does not supply the variable-binding solution, and it says nothing about non-neural implementations or consciousness.
